To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a) we have developed a compiler level intermediate representation (IR) based binary analysis framework that enables the application of well understood compiler level transformations to executables.

(i) we propose the first compiler level representation for executables and demonstrate its effectiveness by employing it in several static analysis frameworks, (ii) we propose the only symbolic analysis framework for binaries in literature that can analyze memory locations and (iii) we devise the only cache locking scheme for general embedded programs in literature that employs cache locking to improve the average case execution time.

(1) a compiler level IR is the most suitable IR for analyzing executables, (2) the absence of higher level semantics in executables is one of the main reasons behind the limited applicability of source level analysis techniques in executables, and (3) the proposed methods for recovering higher level semantics in the IR and defining a precise memory model in executable analysis significantly improves the performance and effectiveness of several traditional analysis techniques in the binary domain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing scalable static binary rewriting methods and analysis using a compiler level intermediate representation.
advancing the state of the art in static binary analysis.
the following contributions: (a) A compiler level IR based binary analysis and rewriting framework.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

this dissertation presents a compiler level intermediate representation for executables, a scalable mechanism for converting executables to such a representation, and a set of novel applications that employ the representation and its analysis.
this dissertation has presented a novel framework that enables the use of compiler level IR in the analysis of executable files.

this thesis has made significant contributions in the field of executable analysis by presenting a compiler level IR for executables, a scalable static binary rewriting mechanism, a precise memory model for executables, and a scalable symbolic analysis framework for binaries.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the work presented in this dissertation is the first to propose an executable level analysis framework that uses the same IR as a compiler.
we have presented a compiler level representation for executable programs that enables several well known compiler level transformations for executables.
we present a novel binary framework that can convert a standalone executable to the same highlevel IR that is used in compilers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a compiler level IR is a powerful abstraction for analyzing executables.
compiler transformations can be successfully applied to executables.
a compiler level IR is an effective representation to perform static analysis and optimizations on executables.
